phonemes.desc: Voiceless bilabial stop [p] followed by open vowel [a]; the first syllable is short and percussive.
Voiced alveolar fricative [z] plus long close back rounded vowel [uː]; the macron marks a reconstructed length in the Akkadian name.
Final voiced alveolar fricative [z] and close back rounded vowel [u]; the name ends with the same syllable it began, giving it a drum-like ring.

pronunciation.approximation: 'pah-ZOO-zoo' — stress the long middle syllable and let the final syllable fall like a dry gust.

pronunciation.note: Pazuzu is Tier 2 because the Unicode restoration preserves only the plain ASCII letters of the Akkadian name; there is no distinctive diacritic or non-ASCII letter that the ASCII form loses. The macron in /paˈzuːzu/ is a scholarly reconstruction of vowel length, not a feature of the written Unicode restoration.

domains.title: PAZUZU — The Wind-Demon Warden
domains.subtitle: Evil Wind · Apotropaic Guardian · Southwest Gale
domains.lead:
Pazuzu is the best-known demon of ancient Mesopotamia: king of the lilû wind-demons, bringer of pestilential winds from the southwest — and, paradoxically, the apotropaic power hung over doorways and cradles to keep worse demons away. He is not merely evil; he is useful evil, a terrifying force turned against other terrifying forces.

This is a domainless flagship: ASCII pazuzu.com is unregistrable; the temple claims no domain ownership.

cards.name: Lord of the Lilû
cards.desc: King of the evil wind-demons in Akkadian and Assyrian incantations; the moving air itself made demonic.

cards.name: Apotropaic Warden
cards.desc: His image was worn to ward off Lamashtu and other child-snatching demons — a frightful guardian against frightful things.

cards.name: Pestilential West Wind
cards.desc: The southwest wind that carried fever, drought, and famine; meteorology and demonology were not separate sciences.

cards.name: Icon of Terror
cards.desc: Leonic face, bulging eyes, serpents, scorpions, and eagle talons — a body designed to be more frightening than the demons it repels.

symbols.name: Serpents and scorpions
symbols.meaning: Attributes of the demon and the poisons he commands; on amulets they also bind Lamashtu.

symbols.name: Leonine face
symbols.meaning: The snarling mask of the wind-demon, meant to out-terrorize any spirit that approaches the threshold.

symbols.name: Eagle talons
symbols.meaning: The grasping, predatory power of the storm-wind and its capacity to snatch life away.

symbols.name: Right hand raised
symbols.meaning: The apotropaic gesture of warding, common on Mesopotamian plaques and demon images.

mythology.lead: Pazuzu has no long narrative epic; his “mythology” is the archive of incantations, amulets, and bronze images that give him a precise job description. He is the demon you invoke when you need a worse demon driven off — a warden whose terror is aimed outward, at Lamashtu and the ill wind, and inward, at the fear itself.

myths.title: Son of Ḫanbi, King of the Evil Wind-Demons
myths.text: Assyrian and Babylonian amulets introduce Pazuzu in the first person, and the self-presentation is itself a document: “I am Pazuzu, son of Ḫanbi, king of the evil lilû-wind-demons.” The formula identifies him as head of a class of wind spirits — the lilû and lilītu whose very names echo down into later Near Eastern lore as Lilith — and gives him a father, Ḫanbi, whose name marks demonic ancestry. The incantations that carry the formula do not ask him to be good; they ask him to work — to rise up, to go at the supplicant’s right hand, to pursue the sickness-demons his juniors have sent. An authority structure is assumed throughout: Pazuzu holds jurisdiction over the air, and every lesser airborne harm answers to his warrant. The ancients did not worship their demons; they deputised them — and the amulet is the warrant, worn on the body like a badge of an invisible police force.

myths.title: The Warden Against Lamashtu
myths.text: Lamashtu was the most feared demoness of the ancient Near East: she attacked pregnant women, strangled newborns, and poisoned the nursing breast. To stop her, families hung Pazuzu amulets and engraved plaques at doorways and bedsides — some plaque types actually bind Lamashtu with snakes and scorpions while the companion inscription instructs the wind-demon-king to frighten her back beneath the earth. The logic is sympathetic magic at its most pragmatic: a demon powerful enough to rule the winds is powerful enough to intimidate a child-killer, and the images show him doing exactly that, grasping serpents while Lamashtu is trussed on a donkey and shipped back to the underworld. Surviving plaques from Assyrian houses still bear the nail-holes of their hanging. This is protective technology in the literal sense — hardware for the nursery, tested by centuries of use, and the clearest proof that Mesopotamian religion managed fear the way engineers manage load: by naming it, and building against it.

myths.title: The Bronze Head from Assyria
myths.text: The most famous Pazuzu image is a bronze head in the Louvre (AO 19931), found in the region of ancient Assyria and dated to the 8th–7th century BCE. It assembles a leonine muzzle, bulging eyes, a scaly brow, a serpentine phallus, and from the back of the head a scorpion’s sting and two pairs of wings — eagle talons were surely part of a now-lost body. Every feature is chosen for maximum fright-value, and the head was meant to be seen, not hidden, because its visibility was the protection: fear, properly aimed, is an instrument. Smaller bronze heads and terracotta figurines repeat the scheme at household scale across Assyria and Babylonia, which is why Assyriologists count Pazuzu among the best-attested demons of the ancient world despite his absence from the great god-lists. His iconography is so consistent that a single unprovenanced head is recognisable at a glance — a brand identity three thousand years deep.

myths.title: The Southwest Wind in Mesopotamian Thought
myths.text: In Mesopotamian thought, certain winds were not weather but agents of disease. The west and southwest winds could bring fever, crop-blight, and the sand-storm — and the medical literature prescribes for their sicknesses much as it prescribes for any other demonic attack. Pazuzu concentrates that dangerous wind into a single persona: when the air itself seems hostile, it helps to name the hostility. He is, in effect, the personification of an ecological anxiety still familiar in hot, dry climates — the dread of the season’s first ill wind. The incantation series Utukku Lemnutu, the “Evil Demons,” maps the whole atmosphere of the ancient city as a population of airborne malevolences, each with a name, a jurisdiction, and a way of being driven off. Pazuzu stands at the head of that map: the demon you invoke when the wind itself turns against you, and naming the wind proves the first step to surviving it.

lore.syncretism:
Pazuzu sits at the intersection of demonology, medicine, and household religion.

His apotropaic role places him alongside other Mesopotamian protective figures such as the apkallu sages and the lion-demon who guards doorways. Later Near Eastern and Mediterranean traditions continued the idea that a demon's own power could be turned against other demons — a logic visible in Jewish and Christian amulets, Gnostic charitēs, and Arabic jinn lore. The modern horror film use of Pazuzu is a 20th-century reinvention; the ancient evidence is overwhelmingly protective, not purely malevolent.
lore.culturalLegacy:
Pazuzu is probably the most visually recognizable Mesopotamian demon in the modern world, but for reasons ancient worshippers would not recognize.

The Louvre bronze head has become an icon of ancient Near Eastern art, reproduced in textbooks, museum merchandise, and popular media. Among Assyriologists, Pazuzu is a case-study in the logic of apotropaic religion: how a culture confronts danger by naming, embodying, and redirecting it. His amulets are early examples of protective technology — a material object designed to keep invisible harm at bay.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Pazuzu teaches that protection and peril can wear the same face. The demon who brings the pestilential wind is the same figure hung over a cradle to guard an infant. This is not contradiction; it is strategy. When the threat is invisible — a fever on the air, a sudden infant death, a miscarriage in the night — the defender must be equally uncanny.

To restore Pazuzu in Unicode is to keep visible the plain, wind-bitten sound of that strategy. There is no glittering diacritic here, no recovered long vowel in the display form. The name is as stark as the desert wind it names. That plainness is itself the point: some powers do not need ornament to be remembered.
sources: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia

lore.archaeology: Pazuzu's material record consists chiefly of bronze heads, terracotta plaques, and engraved amulets from Assyria, Babylonia, and surrounding regions, dated especially to the 8th–7th centuries BCE. The Louvre bronze head (AO 19931) is the most complete example. Amulets depicting Pazuzu opposite Lamashtu were intended for domestic use, often near women and children. Cuneiform incantation tablets give the verbal counterpart to these images, preserving the formulae in which Pazuzu names himself and accepts his apotropaic commission.
lore.cult: Pazuzu had no temple, priest, or festival, and he needed none: his cult was the amulet on the wall and the incantation spoken over it. The evidence is domestic and medical — bronze heads, terracotta plaques, and engraved gems from Assyria and Babylonia, chiefly of the eighth and seventh centuries BCE, placed in houses to guard the people most at risk: women in childbirth and newborns. The pairing is fixed: Pazuzu faces Lamashtu, the child-stealing demon, across the amulet's field, with the bed, the dog, and the donkey of his incantations ranged between them. The cuneiform corpus gives the ritual its voice in striking first-person formulae, in which Pazuzu names himself — son of Ḫanbi, king of the evil wind-demons — and accepts his commission against Lamashtu and her kind. The head-shaped bronzes likely hung by doorways as sentinels. This is apotropaic religion at its purest: no congregation, no calendar, no myth of his deeds — an object that works by existing, a demon hired to fight demons.
lore.iconography: Pazuzu's face was engineered to frighten fever itself. The canonical image is the head: bulging eyes, a wrinkled canine muzzle, open jaws with a lolling tongue, a beard, horns, and the wings of the wind-demon pressed flat above the brow; full-body statuettes add talons, a scorpion's sting, and serpentine members — a body assembled from every predator Mesopotamia could imagine. The Louvre bronze head (AO 19931) is the most complete survivor, its findspot unrecorded — fitting, somehow, for a demon of the air. The type belongs overwhelmingly to the Neo-Assyrian eighth–seventh centuries BCE, with the Lamashtu amulets forming the great series and smaller plaques churned out for household use. The deeper lineage is murkier: the grimacing demons of Old Babylonian glyptic are cousins, not portraits, and no single ancestor claims him. The image did not so much evolve as harden. Once the formula was set, repetition was the point — a hundred identical demons, each one the same wind, each one watching a different cradle.
lore.reception: Pazuzu reached modernity through the ground. Layard's excavations at Nimrud and Nineveh in the 1840s–50s brought demon heads and Lamashtu plaques into the British Museum, while the cuneiform catalogues of evil demons — the Utukku Lemnutu series — entered scholarship through the great text editions of the late nineteenth century. Joining object to incantation was twentieth-century work: scholars matched the bronze heads to the first-person formulae in which Pazuzu names himself, catalogued the Lamashtu amulet series, and Wiggermann's study of the protective spirits and his Reallexikon der Assyriologie article became the modern standard. Between late antiquity and that recovery the trail is cold: unlike Tammuz, Pazuzu survived in no biblical verse or medieval rite — only the broader Near Eastern amulet habit, visible in Jewish, Syriac, and Arabic tradition, preserved the logic of setting one demon to catch another while his own name slept. It is an unusual transmission history for a guardian: he guarded nothing for two thousand years, because the houses that needed him had fallen.
